FARRA:v3p275#2/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p275#2/r5.speaker: عبد الله
FARRA:v3p275#2/r5.claim: ʿAbd Allāh's reading has the phrase once rather than repeated.

FARRA:v3p275#2/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p275#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
FARRA:v3p275#2/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says that one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

MAJAZ:v2p303/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p303/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p303/r2.claim: The repeated promise that ease accompanies hardship makes hope greater than fear.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p380#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p380#3/r1.speaker: الحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p380#3/r1.claim: Hasan says the Prophet joyfully repeated that one hardship will not overcome two eases, citing the verse twice.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p380#3/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p380#3/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p380#3/r2.claim: Ibn Masud says that if hardship were in a burrow, ease would follow to draw it out; one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r1.claim: God promises the Prophet relief alongside the hardship of striving against the polytheists, including eventual victory and their accepting the truth willingly or under compulsion.

TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r2.speaker: النبي ﷺ عن الحسن وقتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r2.claim: The Prophet is reported to reassure his companions that one hardship will not overcome two eases.

TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v24p495#2/r3.claim: Ibn Masud says that even if hardship entered a burrow, ease would follow it, citing the repeated promise.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3446/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3446/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3446/r1.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet said that if hardship entered a stone, ease would follow it in and drive it out; the repeated verse was then revealed.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3446/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3446/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3446/r2.claim: Al-Hasan reports the saying that one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

NAHHAS:v5p252/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p252/r2.speaker: عيسى بن عمر
NAHHAS:v5p252/r2.claim: He reads the sīn in both instances with ḍamma.

NAHHAS:v5p252/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p252/r3.speaker: قيل
NAHHAS:v5p252/r3.claim: One interpretation is that God's favors and ease outnumber hardship.

NAHHAS:v5p252/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p252/r4.speaker: قيل
NAHHAS:v5p252/r4.claim: Another interpretation promises the Prophet victory over the polytheists after the hardship they caused.

SULAMI:v2p405/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p405/r1.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
SULAMI:v2p405/r1.claim: The effort of worldly life is accompanied by the reward of Paradise.

SULAMI:v2p405/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p405/r2.speaker: الجوزجاني
SULAMI:v2p405/r2.claim: Patience in avoiding forbidden and doubtful things brings relief in the dignity of reliance on God.

SULAMI:v2p405/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p405/r3.speaker: القاسم
SULAMI:v2p405/r3.claim: The fortunate pass from the prison of this world to the pleasure of the next, while the wretched remain constrained in both states.

THALABI:v10p233/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p233/r10.speaker: النبي
THALABI:v10p233/r10.claim: After the verse came down, the Prophet told his companions to rejoice: ease had arrived and one hardship would not overcome two eases.

THALABI:v10p233/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p233/r11.speaker: ابن مسعود
THALABI:v10p233/r11.claim: He swears that even if hardship were hidden in a burrow, ease would seek it out; one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

THALABI:v10p233/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p233/r12.speaker: العلماء
THALABI:v10p233/r12.claim: They explain the two-eases saying from Arabic definiteness: repeated definite hardship denotes one, while repeated indefinite ease denotes two.

THALABI:v10p233/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p233/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p233/r8.claim: Repeating the promise confirms it and strengthens hope.

THALABI:v10p233/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p233/r9.speaker: قيل
THALABI:v10p233/r9.claim: Another interpretation assigns the first ease to this world and the repeated ease to the hereafter.

THALABI:v10p234/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r1.speaker: الحسن بن يحيى بن نصر الجرجاني
THALABI:v10p234/r1.claim: He rejects the grammar offered for one hardship and two eases: repeating a definite noun and an indefinite noun does not force one sword but two in the example sentence.

THALABI:v10p234/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r10.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v10p234/r10.claim: He says that with hardship in this world comes the reward of Paradise.

THALABI:v10p234/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r11.speaker: القاسم
THALABI:v10p234/r11.claim: He describes the gladness of this happiness as extending from the dawn hours of worldly life to the pleasure of the afterlife.

THALABI:v10p234/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r12.speaker: قراءة العامة
THALABI:v10p234/r12.claim: The common reading pronounces the sīn lightly in both repetitions of yusr.

THALABI:v10p234/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r13.speaker: أبو جعفر وعيسى
THALABI:v10p234/r13.claim: They read both instances with a damma on the sīn.

THALABI:v10p234/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r14.speaker: قراءة عبد الله
THALABI:v10p234/r14.claim: The codex attributed to Abdullah has the ease clause only once, without repetition.

THALABI:v10p234/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p234/r2.claim: The saying means one hardship cannot overcome both promised eases; it can overcome worldly ease, but the hereafter’s lasting ease cannot be defeated.

THALABI:v10p234/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p234/r7.claim: The second clause begins a separate favor for the hereafter; lacking a conjunction, it generalizes to believers, whose worldly hardship is surely followed by ease in the next life.

THALABI:v10p234/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p234/r8.claim: The hadith means the single worldly hardship cannot overcome both the worldly ease promised to the Prophet and the enduring ease promised to believers in the hereafter.

THALABI:v10p234/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p234/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p234/r9.claim: He compares this wording to the two feast months not both being diminished: two things are not jointly overcome by one event.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r17.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r17.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r17.claim: Mawardi says hardship may accompany the good of the afterlife, or relief, spaciousness, and happiness may accompany hardship, patience, and adversity.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r18.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r18.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r18.claim: He allows that God may grant ease alongside hardship, that worldly hardship may have ease in the afterlife, or that the tested person who perseveres may receive contentment or abundance.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r19.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r19.speaker: ابن مسعود
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r19.claim: Ibn Masud swears that if hardship were in a rock, ease would seek it out and enter; one hardship will not overcome two eases.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r20.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r20.speaker: ثعلب
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r20.claim: Thalab explains the repetition as one definite hardship and two indefinite eases, strengthening hope and encouraging patience.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r21.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r21.speaker: الفراء
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p296#2/r21.claim: Al-Farra says the repeated phrase is rhetorical elaboration and emphasis, like repeating yes or no in an answer; he cites a poem.

QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r15.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r15.speaker: الخبر
QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r15.claim: A report says that one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r16.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r16.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r16.claim: The repeated definite “hardship” refers to one known hardship, while the two indefinite instances of “ease” indicate two distinct eases.

QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r17.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r17.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r17.claim: The single hardship is worldly adversity; the two eases are worldly prosperity and relief from trials, followed by reward in the afterlife.

QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r18.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r18.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p432/r18.claim: All believers share the hardship of worldly trials, while their two eases are relief in this life and recompense tomorrow.

WAHIDI-QT:94:6/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:94:6/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:94:6/r1.claim: One reading treats the repetition as emphasis; another makes a general promise of relief to every believer in this life or the next, counting one hardship and two eases.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:94:1-6/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:94:1-6/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:94:1-6/r5.claim: The repetition emphasizes assurance; another reading generalizes the promise to every hardship, with ease in this life or the next, and says one hardship has two eases.

JISHUMI:v10p7463/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7463/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر
JISHUMI:v10p7463/r3.claim: He reads the sīn in both occurrences of yusran with ḍamma; the common reading has sukūn.

JISHUMI:v10p7463/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7463/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
JISHUMI:v10p7463/r4.claim: A report in his name gives “with hardship is ease” once rather than repeating it, but the author says it cannot be relied on because it is an isolated report.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r1.claim: The hardship is the Prophet's struggle against polytheists, and its accompanying ease is his eventual triumph as they submit to the truth he brought.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r10.speaker: أبو علي الحسن بن يحيى بن نصر الجرجاني
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r10.claim: Al-Jurjani reads the second clause as a fresh promise of an afterlife benefit for all believers; its lack of an introductory conjunction marks the new beginning.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r2.claim: Repeating the promise of ease confirms it and magnifies hope.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r3.speaker: الحسن
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r3.claim: Hasan reports that on revelation the Prophet announced that ease had arrived and hardship would not overcome two eases.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r4.claim: Ibn Masud says that even if hardship were inside a stone, ease would seek it out and enter; hardship cannot overcome two eases.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r5.claim: The commentators explain the saying through Arabic usage: repeated definite al-usr refers to one hardship, while repeated indefinite yusr denotes two eases.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r6.speaker: أبو علي الحسن بن يحيى بن نصر الجرجاني
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r6.claim: Al-Jurjani rejects the claim that definiteness and indefiniteness alone prove one hardship and two eases; repeating a definite noun does not force one referent and an indefinite noun two.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r7.speaker: أبو علي الحسن بن يحيى بن نصر الجرجاني
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p464#2/r7.claim: Al-Jurjani illustrates his objection with the repeated phrase about a horse and a sword, which does not entail one horse but two swords.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r1.claim: 'With' presents relief as accompanying hardship by drawing near the ease God will bring soon, consoling people and strengthening their hearts.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r10.claim: Ibn Masud's codex has the ease clause only once.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r11.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r11.speaker: النبي
KASHSHAF:94:6/r11.claim: A prophetic report says that if hardship were in a lizard's hole, ease would seek it out, and hardship would not overcome two eases.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r12.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r12.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r12.claim: The Prophet's two eases can be understood as the magnified ease in the verse applied to both abodes, making two in reality despite Ibn Masud's single written occurrence.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r2.speaker: ابن عباس وابن مسعود
KASHSHAF:94:6/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Masud say hardship cannot overcome two eases; the statement is also reported as a prophetic saying.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r3.speaker: النبي
KASHSHAF:94:6/r3.claim: A report says the Prophet once came out laughing and declared that hardship would not overcome two eases; no grading is given.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r4.claim: The saying follows the apparent wording and strong hope, taking God's promise in its fullest and most generous sense.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r5.claim: The repeated sentence may simply reinforce the first promise in people's hearts, like repeating the warning 'woe that day to the deniers.'

KASHSHAF:94:6/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r6.claim: Alternatively, the first sentence promises ease after their known hardship and the second gives a fresh promise of further ease, yielding two eases.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r7.claim: The definite singular hardship is one hardship whether it refers to their known affliction or to hardship as a familiar kind.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r8.claim: The two eases may be victories during the Prophet's lifetime and the caliphs' eras, or ease in this world and the next, like the two good outcomes in another verse.

KASHSHAF:94:6/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:94:6/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:94:6/r9.claim: The indefinite yusran conveys magnification: the promised ease is immense and extraordinary.

TABRISI:94:4-6/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:94:4-6/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:94:4-6/r12.claim: The second ease begins a new statement for all believers: hardship here is joined by ease in the afterlife, and sometimes both worldly and afterlife relief.

QURTUBI-FULL:94:5-6/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:94:5-6/r13.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:94:5-6/r13.claim: The second, conjunction-free sentence begins a distinct promise of afterlife relief for every believer alongside worldly hardship; the lack of a coordinating particle supports its independence.

QURTUBI-FULL:94:5-6/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:94:5-6/r14.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:94:5-6/r14.claim: Every believer's worldly hardship will certainly be accompanied by ease in the afterlife, though ease in both lives may coincide.

BAYDAWI-FULL:94:4-6/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:94:4-6/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:94:4-6/r3.claim: The repetition either emphasizes the promise or promises a second ease, such as afterlife reward; definite عسر remains one instance while indefinite يسر may be another, as in the report that two eases cannot be overcome by one hardship.

BAYDAWI-FULL:94:4-6/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:94:4-6/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:94:4-6/r4.claim: The Prophet said one hardship will never overcome two eases.

QASHANI:94:5-7/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:94:5-7/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:94:5-7/r1.claim: The two hardships are veiling by creation from God and then by God from creation; their eases are disclosure of the Essence with sainthood and divinely given expansion with prophethood.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p500/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p500/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p500/r7.claim: The enumerated favors imply victory over enemies; the promise of ease also counters unbelievers' mockery of the believers' poverty and assures prompt relief after hardship.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p500/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p500/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p500/r8.claim: The repeated promise most clearly emphasizes relief; other readings distinguish relief in this life and the next, or two eases because the definite hardship is one and the indefinite ease another.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p501/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p501/r1.speaker: الرسول
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p501/r1.claim: A prophetic report says one hardship will not overcome two eases.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p501/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p501/r2.speaker: ابن وثاب وأبو جعفر وعيسى
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p501/r2.claim: Ibn Waththāb, Abū Jaʿfar, and ʿĪsā pronounce the sīn of ʿusr and yusr with ḍamma; the majority use sukūn.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r1.claim: God states and then reinforces that ease exists alongside hardship.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r2.claim: The Prophet says that if hardship entered a stone, ease would come in after it and drive it out; the report from Anas is weak according to Abu Hatim.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r3.claim: Shubah transmits the saying that one hardship cannot overcome two eases as a statement stopped at Ibn Masud.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r4.claim: Early authorities say one hardship cannot defeat two eases; al-Hasan reports that the Prophet cheerfully repeated this assurance, with additional mursal routes.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r5.claim: Qatadah says the Prophet gave his companions glad tidings from these verses that one hardship would not overcome two eases.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p431#2/r6.claim: The single definite word for hardship in both verses refers to one hardship, while the indefinite ease is repeated as two distinct eases.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r1.claim: The Prophet says heavenly aid comes in proportion to burdens and patience in proportion to affliction, in a report transmitted from Abu Hurayrah.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r2.speaker: الشافعي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r2.claim: Al-Shafii's poem encourages beautiful patience and says those who watch God in their affairs are saved and find relief near.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r3.speaker: ابن دريد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r3.claim: Ibn Duraid quotes Abu Hatim al-Sijistani's poem: when every avenue appears closed, divine relief arrives at the point of despair and hardship is followed by near deliverance.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p432/r4.claim: Further anonymous poetry says relief appears after calamities reach their tightest point, though the sufferer may think no escape remains.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r10.speaker: عمر
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r10.claim: ʿUmar sent Abū ʿUbayda in Syria the saying that one hardship would not defeat two eases; Ibn Ḥajar considers this report’s route the strongest.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r11.speaker: سعد الدين التفتازاني
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r11.claim: Al-Taftāzānī lays out four cases for repeating a noun as definite or indefinite, with a repeated indefinite ordinarily indicating a different referent and a definite the same one.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r12.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r12.claim: The author rejects the grammatical rule as absolute: definiteness need not mean totality, context can defeat identity, and a repeated definite can refer to something different.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r4.claim: The second statement answers those asking what follows hardship; its repeated definite al-ʿusr denotes the same hardship, while the indefinite ease is another ease.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r5.speaker: الحسن البصري
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r5.claim: Al-Ḥasan reports that, when the verse was revealed, the Prophet said that one hardship would not overcome two eases.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r6.speaker: ابن مسعود
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r6.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says that if hardship were in a lizard’s hole, ease would follow it until bringing it out.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r7.speaker: ابن مسعود
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r7.claim: A Prophetic version from Ibn Masʿūd says ease would enter even a lizard’s hole; al-Haythamī grades its chain weak because it contains Abū Mālik al-Nakhaʿī.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r8.speaker: أنس
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r8.claim: Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bazzār report a similar saying from Anas; al-Haythamī calls its chain weak because it contains ʿĀʾidh ibn Shurayḥ.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
BIQAI-FULL:v8p463/r9.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet came out smiling and repeated that one hardship would not defeat two eases.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r1.claim: The usual rule is only a default without contextual clues: repeating a definite normally preserves its referent, while a repeated indefinite normally changes it.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r2.claim: Repeated definite nouns can change referent; the examples include scripture, enmity, ranks, and a requested book, while a poet’s repeated “time” would be pointless if identical.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r3.claim: An indefinite noun can repeat with the same referent, as in God being deity in heaven and earth, a requested sign, and human weakness followed by strength and weakness.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r4.claim: A definite noun after an indefinite one can change scope: reconciliation for spouses becomes reconciliation generally, and punishment is added to prior punishment.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p465/r5.claim: A definite noun may recur with a different referent, as when a later scripture confirms an earlier scripture.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r1.speaker: أبو جعفر بن الزبير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r1.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr links this surah to the two preceding ones: human form seems to promise shared perfection, yet people diverge toward ascent or degradation.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر بن الزبير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r2.claim: Those who rise answer a divine call quickly, while people who resist follow what was written for them; each person is made ready for the end appointed to them.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر بن الزبير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r3.claim: A fair-minded person should know that everyone is enabled for the end they were created for and should ask God for sincerity; whoever finds good should thank God.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#2/r4.claim: The surah explains the Prophet's abundant favors and signs of divine love: God neither forsook nor disliked him, and bestowed these gifts by grace rather than earned merit.

DURR-FULL:v8p549/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p549/r5.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p549/r5.claim: The Prophet gave his companions glad tidings from these verses, saying one hardship will not overcome two eases.

DURR-FULL:v8p549/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p549/r6.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p549/r6.claim: When the verse was revealed, the Prophet announced that ease had come and one hardship would not overcome two eases.

DURR-FULL:v8p549/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p549/r7.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
DURR-FULL:v8p549/r7.claim: On a 300-person expedition with only two sacks of dates, the Prophet reassured them that God had inspired the promise of ease and sent a companion to announce it.

DURR-FULL:v8p550/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r1.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r1.claim: The Prophet said that if hardship entered a rock, ease would enter after it and drive it out; the passage was revealed.

DURR-FULL:v8p550/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r2.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r2.claim: At Baqiʿ al-Farqad, the Prophet repeated that if hardship entered a rock, ease would follow and expel it; the verse came down.

DURR-FULL:v8p550/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r3.claim: In a weak-chain report, the Prophet said ease would enter a rock to expel hardship, then recited the verse.

DURR-FULL:v8p550/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r4.claim: He said that if hardship were in a rock, ease would pursue it and enter to expel it; one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

DURR-FULL:v8p550/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r5.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r5.claim: The Prophet came out delighted and laughing, saying one hardship would not overcome two eases.

DURR-FULL:v8p550/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r6.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p550/r6.claim: He reports the saying that one hardship does not overcome two eases.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p232/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p232/r1.speaker: author
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p232/r1.claim: The verses were said to have been revealed when polytheists taunted Muslims for their poverty.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p232/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p232/r2.speaker: الحسن
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p232/r2.claim: Al-Hasan reports that when “with hardship comes ease” was revealed, the Prophet announced that ease had come and one hardship would never overcome two eases.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r10.speaker: رسول الله
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r10.claim: The Prophet says the most severely tested are the prophets, then the saints, then the people nearest them in virtue.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r11.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r11.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r11.claim: The author links persistence in prayer to God's call to invoke Him and to a report that God loves those who persistently supplicate.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r12.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r12.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r12.claim: The definite hardship and indefinite ease hint that worldly life is known as a home of hardship, while its ease is less familiar; the repeated sentence either emphasizes the promise or announces another ease accompanying the hardship.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r4.claim: The repeated promise explains the preceding divine favors and assures the Prophet and believers that every difficulty will be eased; the definite hardship is universal, and “with” signals that ease comes swiftly, as if alongside hardship.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r5.speaker: الكشاف
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r5.claim: Al-Kashshaf says the polytheists mocked the Prophet and believers for poverty, so the Prophet feared they might leave Islam; God recalled His great favors and promised abundant ease.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r6.claim: Although opposites ordinarily succeed rather than coexist, the wording “with hardship” conveys the rapid arrival of ease as though it accompanied hardship.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r7.claim: A common reading understands companionship figuratively, while an elite reading takes the companionship as real.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r8.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r8.claim: Ibn al-‘Arabi calls it coexistence through intermixture rather than simple pairing or succession: ease must exist in hardship to prevent ruin, hardship must exist in ease for contrast, and all hardship ultimately becomes ease.

BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r9.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
BURSEVI:v10p356#3/r9.claim: Divine mercy precedes wrath; hardship can polish and expand the hearts of spiritual elites so they become ready for divine self-disclosure.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r1.claim: The second sentence may repeat the first to reinforce it or make a fresh promise; if fresh, its ease may be what came under the caliphs or the ease of the afterlife.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r10.claim: If both clauses refer to the same hardship but two distinct eases, the result is two great eases accompanying each hardship, likely worldly and afterlife relief.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r11.claim: Others take the second sentence as an exact repetition, comparing it to saying the horse has a spear twice; the hadith does not prove a new promise because one magnified ease can span both realms.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r12.claim: The common figurative reading treats مع as meaning after, stressing the close succession of ease to hardship.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r13.claim: The author raises cases where hardship is not followed by worldly ease or afterlife reward, including lasting illness and the impatient believer.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r14.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r14.claim: Restricting the promise to believers fits consolation, but does not solve cases where a believer's hardship brings no worldly ease or a despairing believer earns no afterlife reward.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r15.claim: Proposed answers include customary rather than universal scope, restriction to the patient believer, or conditioning the promise on God's will.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r16.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r16.claim: A report says the Prophet assured his companions, if God wills, that one hardship would not overcome two eases.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r17.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r17.claim: Another reading takes the indefinite ease as a kind of ease, so no hardship lacks some relief, at least protection from something worse; it may also denote such greater relief.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r18.speaker: ابن الفارض
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r18.claim: A mystical reading says the beloved's acts are sweet to the lover, including suffering; the author dismisses the claim as strained.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r2.claim: The author prefers a fresh promise because establishing a new meaning is more eloquent than repetition and best suits consolation.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r3.speaker: عصام الدين
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r3.claim: He suggests that the lack of a conjunction may be apt because the second sentence appears as a repetition; the author counters that no special explanation is needed.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r4.claim: The repeated ease is indefinite for magnification and to suggest a newly promised ease; repeating an indefinite noun normally signals difference.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r5.speaker: الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r5.claim: A report says the Prophet came out smiling and said one hardship will not overcome two eases, reciting both verses.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r6.claim: A scholar reads the passage as a promise that every difficulty will be eased; the definite hardship is comprehensive and the ease is great.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r7.claim: On that reading, hardships such as constriction, a burdensome load, and obscurity are paired with expansion, relief of the burden, and elevated renown.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r8.claim: Some call the fa causal; another calls it inferential, as when examples of chewing animals support a general rule.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p170/r9.claim: The second sentence likewise admits repetition or a fresh promise, with the fresh-promise reading preferred for the stated reasons.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r1.speaker: أنس بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r1.claim: A report says the Prophet pointed to a stone and said ease would follow hardship even into it; this supports close accompaniment, but the author sees literal co-presence as unlikely.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r2.claim: Reading العسر as a particular known hardship avoids the dispute, though the apparent context points to general scope; general scope needs the condition of trust and hope in God.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r3.claim: A general reading should be qualified for those facing hardship with trust in God, good hope, and wholehearted reliance.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p171/r4.claim: Ibn Waththāb, Abū Jaʿfar, and ʿĪsā read al-ʿusr and yusr with a ḍamma on the sīn in both occurrences.

ELMALILI:94:5-6/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r10.speaker: Zeyd b. Eslem، Ebû Ubeyde، Ömer b. Hattâb
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r10.claim: In a report through Zayd b. Aslam, Abu ʿUbayda wrote ʿUmar about the Romans; ʿUmar replied that God brings relief after hardship in a believer's heart and hardship cannot defeat two eases.

ELMALILI:94:5-6/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r11.claim: Calling it a believer's heart points to faith's tranquility and patience; a believer's lamentation and loss of afterlife reward do not invalidate the promise, whose fulfillment remains subject to God's will.

ELMALILI:94:5-6/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r4.claim: The repeated statement confirms the first promise and generalizes it: whoever confronts hardship with faith and patient endurance by God's permission reaches its ease.

ELMALILI:94:5-6/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r5.claim: Maʿa can mean baʿda because hardship and ease succeed one another, as also expressed by the promise that God will bring ease after hardship.

ELMALILI:94:5-6/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r6.claim: They can also be considered simultaneous from different aspects: what seems difficult from one angle may contain an easier aspect that can be found and acted upon.

ELMALILI:94:5-6/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r7.claim: Believers who affirm the good and act accordingly have two kinds of ease in every hardship, one worldly and one otherworldly.

ELMALILI:94:5-6/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r8.speaker: رسول الله
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r8.claim: When the verses descended, the Prophet came out smiling and said that one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

ELMALILI:94:5-6/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:94:5-6/r9.claim: The familiar grammatical explanation counts one definite hardship and two indefinite eases, though the author also derives the point from the verses' links to their context.

QUTB-ZILAL:94:6/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:94:6/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:94:6/r1.claim: The repeated promise strongly emphasizes reassurance; its repetition suggests that the Prophet faced severe hardship and needed repeated reminders of divine care and its signs.

QUTB-ZILAL:94:6/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:94:6/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:94:6/r2.claim: A concern heavy enough to weigh on Muhammad so much must have been immense.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p413/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p413/r8.speaker: الحسن
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p413/r8.claim: A report through Yunus and Maʿmar from al-Hasan attributes to the Prophet the glad tidings that ease has come and one hardship cannot overcome two eases; Ibn Ashur takes this as including the community.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p413/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p413/r9.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p413/r9.claim: In the Muwatta, Abu Ubayda wrote Umar about Roman forces and fears; Umar replied that God gives a believing servant relief after hardship and one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r1.speaker: عائذ بن شريح
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r1.claim: Aʿidh ibn Shurayh reports from Anas that the Prophet said if hardship entered a rock, ease would enter after it and drive hardship out; then the two verses were revealed.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r2.speaker: البزار
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r2.claim: Al-Bazzar says he knows no transmitter of this Anas report except Aʿidh ibn Shurayh.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r3.speaker: أبو حاتم الرازي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r3.claim: Abu Hatim al-Razi judged the Aʿidh ibn Shurayh hadith weak, as quoted by Ibn Kathir.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r4.claim: Ibn Jarir transmits a similar report from Ibn Masʿud as a Companion statement, not as a prophetic report.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas reports the divine saying that God created one hardship and two eases, so hardship cannot overcome both.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p414/r9.claim: Some exegetes assign worldly ease to the first clause and afterlife ease to the second, but the Arabic structure makes the latter pure emphasis.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r1.claim: The rule that a repeated definite noun is identical and an indefinite one different does not establish “two eases”: it concerns an indefinite later made definite by the covenant article, in another sentence.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r2.speaker: أبو علي الحسين الجرجاني
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r2.claim: Abu Ali al-Husayn al-Jurjani had already refuted that grammatical argument in al-Nazm; al-Kashshaf also rejects it, and Ibn Hisham calls the rule mistaken.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r3.claim: The second sentence emphasizes the judgment that ease accompanies hardship; “two eases” is a symbolic dual for ease's preponderance, not a count derived from definiteness.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r4.claim: The dual can suggest repeated abundance: as “look twice” in al-Mulk means look repeatedly, and expressions such as labbayk use repetition that implies strength.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p415/r5.claim: The “one hardship, two eases” interpretation is not derived from the definite article on hardship or the indefinite form of ease.

TABATABAI:94:5-8/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:94:5-8/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:94:5-8/r3.claim: Repeating the sentence confirms and strengthens it; treating it as a new sentence is another view. The claim that one definite hardship yields two separate eases relies on a grammatical rule that is not universal.

ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r1.claim: Ash-Sharh was revealed almost immediately after Ad-Duha and appears to continue it directly.

ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r2.speaker: Ta'us ibn Kaysan and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz
ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r2.claim: They regarded Ad-Duha and Ash-Sharh as one surah and recited them in prayer without a second basmala; Asad cites Razi.

ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r3.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r3.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:94:intro/r3.claim: The surah addresses the Prophet first and, through him, every true follower of the Qur'an.

BINTSHATI:v1p68/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p68/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p68/r3.claim: The fa links ease causally to the prior gifts of expanded breast, removed burden, and raised mention; inna and repetition reinforce reassurance and remove doubt.

BINTSHATI:v1p68/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p68/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p68/r4.claim: Repetition in short surahs need not be rhetorical excess when the occasion calls for reinforcing assurance.

BINTSHATI:v1p69/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says ma'a makes relief follow hardship soon, so that the coming ease is treated as if accompanying it for comfort.

BINTSHATI:v1p69/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r2.speaker: النيسابوري
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r2.claim: Al-Nisaburi likewise says nearness makes the time of ease seem continuous with hardship and strengthens hope.

BINTSHATI:v1p69/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r3.speaker: الشيخ محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r3.claim: Abduh says ma'a secures hope that relief must come, as though already with hardship.

BINTSHATI:v1p69/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r4.claim: The author agrees that ma'a signals accompaniment but rejects the simile and the generalization to believers: the context chiefly reassures the Prophet, and the ease is joined to hardship.

BINTSHATI:v1p69/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r5.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
BINTSHATI:v1p69/r5.claim: They argue that repeated definite al-usr refers to one known hardship, while the indefinite yusr presents two distinct eases; a report from the Prophet says one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

BINTSHATI:v1p70/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p70/r1.speaker: أبو حيان
BINTSHATI:v1p70/r1.claim: Al-Bahr reports the view that one hardship comes with two eases because hardship is definite and ease indefinite.

BINTSHATI:v1p70/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p70/r2.speaker: الجرجاني
BINTSHATI:v1p70/r2.claim: Al-Jurjani warns that repeating a sentence about a horse with a sword does not prove the horse has two swords.

BINTSHATI:v1p70/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p70/r3.speaker: النيسابوري
BINTSHATI:v1p70/r3.claim: Al-Nisaburi explores generic or definite hardship and repeated or new sentences, concluding that a sound hadith would require one hardship and two distinct eases; without it, several readings remain possible.

BINTSHATI:v1p70/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p70/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p70/r4.claim: The author finds the competing grammatical scenarios needlessly complex; some commentators also identify the two eases as worldly and afterlife relief or as conquests and afterlife reward.

BINTSHATI:v1p71/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p71/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p71/r1.claim: The second verse confirms the first to strengthen the Prophet's inward certainty in God's gifts, rather than introduce a separate promise.

BINTSHATI:v1p71/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p71/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p71/r2.claim: Al-usr is definite by reference to the Prophet's distress at facing entrenched idolatry, while indefinite yusr leaves the relief open rather than setting limits on it.

BINTSHATI:v1p71/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p71/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p71/r3.claim: Usr denotes the most severe hardship and struggle, with Arabic usage for intense physical constriction and Qur'anic descriptions of the Day's hardship and other acute trials.

BINTSHATI:v1p72/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p72/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p72/r1.claim: Yusr is the opposite of hardship; Arabic also uses it for wealth and for something prepared or achieved without difficulty, conveying relief and release here.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r1.claim: Sūrah Alam Nashraḥ completes the preceding sūrah: 93:6’s sheltering and other favours concerned the period before and just after prophethood, while this sūrah points to blessings after Islam spread in Arabia.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r2.claim: The prior sūrah predicts a bright future; this one points to predictions already beginning to materialize and assures the Prophet that hardship yields to success if faced courageously.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p363/r3.claim: The discourse proceeds from inner expansion, through the recurring law of hardship with relief, to completion of the mission and disciplined use of its success.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r1.claim: These verses teach the Prophet to endure affliction patiently: earlier hardship was followed by relief, and the same divine pattern will continue through the mission.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r3.speaker: most commentators
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r3.claim: Most commentators take the repeated statement as mere emphasis.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p366/r4.claim: Islahi rejects mere emphatic repetition: hardship and ease coexist and recur in cycles, so each success is followed by further trials requiring continued struggle on the path of truth.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p367/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p367/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p367/r1.claim: Those who remain steadfast through trials receive renewed ease after each difficulty, helping them continue toward their ultimate destination.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p367/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p367/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p367/r2.claim: Trials distinguish the righteous from hypocrites and believers from disbelievers, so reward and punishment follow deeds without grounds for a complaint of injustice.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r1.claim: In Mecca, the Prophet and believers suffered growing polytheist persecution, even torture, which grieved them.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r2.claim: These verses consoled the Prophet and believers and promised relief and success after hardship.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r3.speaker: Hz. Peygamber
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:94:5/r3.claim: On the surah's revelation, the Prophet noted that ease is mentioned twice alongside hardship and told believers that one hardship can never overcome two eases.

QIRAAT-ER:94:6:3#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:94:6:3#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:94:6:3#1/r1.claim: Vocalizing the medial consonant with ḍamma is a dialectal variant that preserves meaning.

QIRAAT-ER:94:6:4#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:94:6:4#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:94:6:4#1/r1.claim: Full yusuran vocalization parallels al-ʿusuri as a dialectal variant with no semantic change.

STUDYQURAN:94:5/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:94:5/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:94:5/r1.claim: The verses can mean that patiently enduring hardship brings ease in both this life and the Hereafter.

STUDYQURAN:94:5/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:94:5/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:94:5/r2.claim: A well-known hadith says one instance of hardship never overcomes two instances of ease.

STUDYQURAN:94:5/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:94:5/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:94:5/r3.claim: The claim is linked to God's promise to bring ease after hardship and desire ease rather than hardship for people.

STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r1.speaker: most commentators
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r1.claim: Most call al-Sharḥ Makkan and place it just after Sūrah 93; Ibn ʿAbbās calls it Madinan, while some assign only vv. 5–6 to Madinah.

STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r3.claim: Some say Sūrahs 93 and 94 were originally one, since Companions recited them together in one prayer cycle without a basmalah separating them.

STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:94:intro/r5.claim: Both sūrahs present God's bounties as relief: Sūrah 93 addresses external needs, Sūrah 94 spiritual relief; 94 recalls blessings, reassures, then commands exertion and turning to God.
